difficultyRationale: A subtle but common production pitfall: coordinating timeouts across hops, not just setting one on each call in isolation.
prompt: Service A calls service B with a 5-second timeout. B, to handle that request, calls service C — and B's own timeout on that call to C is also set to 5 seconds. Under load, requests to A sometimes take close to 10 seconds to fail even though every individual timeout is 5 seconds. What's going wrong, and how should timeouts across a call chain actually be set?
explanation: If B's call to C can take up to 5 seconds to time out, and only then does B respond to A (possibly after its own processing), the total time A can wait is the sum of C's timeout plus whatever B still has to do — which can approach or exceed A's own 5-second budget without any single timeout technically being wrong. Each hop's timeout needs to fit inside the remaining budget of the hop that called it, so a later timeout can never by itself exceed the time its caller is still willing to wait.

options.text: Each hop's own timeout needs to fit inside the remaining time budget of whichever call invoked it; here B's timeout on C (5s) leaves no room within A's 5s budget, so the total chain can approach double, which is exactly the delay being observed.
options.explanation: Correct. Timeouts must be coordinated down the call chain, not set identically and independently at each hop — B's call to C has to time out well before A's own patience runs out, or A ends up waiting on the sum of both.

options.text: Since both timeouts are individually set to exactly 5 seconds, this is actually impossible under normal network conditions — the 10-second delays described must be caused by retry logic at B, not by how the two timeouts relate to each other.
options.explanation: Two independent 5-second timeouts stacked in sequence (A waiting on B, B waiting on C) genuinely can add up to roughly 10 seconds with no retries involved at all; dismissing it as impossible ignores how sequential timeouts compose.

options.text: Timeouts only apply to the network transport layer, not to how long a service spends processing after a call returns, so B's 5-second timeout on C has no bearing on how long A ultimately waits — the delay must come from A's own processing instead.
options.explanation: A service waiting for its downstream call to either return or time out is waiting on exactly that duration before it can respond to its own caller; the downstream timeout absolutely does factor into the upstream caller's total wait.

options.text: The fix is to remove B's timeout on its call to C entirely, since B should always wait as long as it takes for C to answer rather than fail early — removing the inner timeout eliminates the compounding delay seen at A.
options.explanation: Removing B's timeout on C doesn't bound anything — it just lets B wait indefinitely on C, which makes A's eventual failure take even longer rather than shorter; the fix is a shorter, coordinated inner timeout, not none at all.

references.title: Google Site Reliability Engineering book — Addressing Cascading Failures (deadline/timeout propagation across a call chain)
